newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha resigns, parliament to meet.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha resigns, parliament to meet.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha resigned on Wednesday shortly before the first meeting of a new parliament dominated by his Socialist opponents.
In a letter to the legislature, Berisha said he had stepped down to take a seat as an opposition deputy for his Democratic Party, which suffered a resounding defeat in elections on June 29.
"I declare today my irrevocable resignation from the post of head of state to continue political parliamentary life supporting the values and the alternative I believe in," Berisha said.

The news was greeted with celebratory gunshots in Tirana and in anti-Berisha strongholds like Berat and the southern port of Vlore, the flashpoint of protests in March over the collapse of high-interest pyramid investment schemes.

"The financial pyramid scheme crisis, of course a negative phenomenon of our governing, was exploited as a pretext by the former Albanian communists to organise an armed communist rebellion," Berisha said.
The new parliament marked "the return to power of the last communist nomenklatura".
"The hours to come will give the possibility to all Albanians coldbloodedly to consider once again the five years of democracy and the five months of rebellion," he said.
Parliament is expected to elect Socialist Party secretary general Rexhep Mejdani as president to replace Berisha.

Following constitutional court rulings on disputes and some changing of alliances, the Socialists and their coalition allies will have 118 seats in the 155-seat parliament, while the Democrats have 24.
The Democrats said they would boycott Wednesday's session to protest at the conduct of the poll, which was described by international monitors as acceptable, if far from perfect.

They complain the elections were held in a climate of terror and they were unable to campaign in the south. But diplomats say their losses even in Tirana put paid to any serious claims of manipulation.
The new assembly was dubbed the "parliament of Kalashnikovs" by pro-Berisha newspapers on Wednesday, and "the parliament of hope" by pro-Socialist dailies.
Koha Jone's front page had a photograph of a wild-eyed Berisha giving a stiff-armed Hitler salute to a rally with the headline "July 23, 1997 - The end of the dictatorships".

Berisha, a former communist heart surgeon, was initially praised in the West for rapid introduction of market reforms. But enthusiasm faded as he resorted to increasingly authoritarian methods and failed to check the spread of the pyramid schemes.
His government resigned in March at the height of unrest in which more than 1,500 people were killed.
The first tasks of the new assembly will be to restore law and order and to resolve the economic chaos left by the collapse of the pyramid schemes.

Armouries were looted at the start of the unrest. The security situation is becoming more precarious with the gradual withdrawal of international peacekeepers who deployed in April to protect the election process and guard aid deliveries. All the 7,000 troops are expected to be gone by mid-August.
An explosion wrecked two cafes in Tirana early on Tuesday and army sources said thieves had stolen missiles thought to be Chinese-made Silkworms from a depot near the Greek border.

Democracy has shaky foundations in Albania, where Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha ruled with an iron fist for 40 years until his death in April 1985, crushing opposition and isolating his state under a policy of self-reliance.

His successor, communist President Ramiz Alia, ruled out change, but a wave of anti-government demonstrations from July 1990 gradually led to reforms, culminating in multi-party elections in March 1991.
